sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: Sleep is necessary for optimal functioning and for overall health and wellbeing. You might have heard advice on how to improve your sleep, such as reducing intense activities close to bedtime or keeping a regular sleep-and-wake schedule. As many countries experience climate change, it is also important to be aware of how sleep may be affected when the temperature changes. Sleep may be delayed or disturbed in a cold environment or a hot and humid one, and poor sleep can make it difficult to function well, especially if it happens often. It is important to create a good sleep environment, keeping in mind that the temperature and humidity of the room, the air circulation, as well as the bedding and clothes worn to bed, play a role in a person’s ability to get the most out of the time spent in bed.

sections.heading: The Ins And Outs of Sleep
paragraphs: Like personal hygiene, sleep hygiene is important for your physical and mental health. Good sleep hygiene habits include a regular bedtime and wake-up time, and sleeping in a dark and quiet environment free from distractions. But how about the temperature in your bedroom? Can changes in room temperature disrupt your sleep? Many studies suggest that they can.

Sleep consists of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep. NREM is the sleep that you first enter when you go to bed at night. It consists of three stages, with each one reflecting a deeper level of sleep. In the final stage, your brain activity slows down a lot compared to wakefulness, and it is called slow-wave sleep (SWS). SWS is important because it supports memory, immune function, and helps you feel refreshed the next day. REM sleep is characterized by intense brain activity and rapid eye movements, thus the name. During REM, you mostly dream, so you can think of it as dream sleep. REM sleep is important for brain development and the processing of emotions. Each night, you cycle through these stages of sleep several times until you wake up the next day \[1\].

sections.heading: The Thermal Environment Around Sleep
paragraphs: Your body temperature and the room temperature are the two main components of the thermal environment for sleep. However, the airflow in the room, the type of bedding you use, and the clothing you wear to bed can also contribute to the thermal environment and affect sleep. Researchers have tried to find the best temperature for humans to sleep in, but this has proven difficult. In laboratory settings, when people slept with minimal clothing and no bedding, the optimal temperature for sleep was found to be at 29°C (84.2°F) \[2\]. However, when you sleep at home, you probably use bedding and may wear pajamas, so this temperature may be too high. Several studies investigated sleep and temperature when people slept in their homes and found that sleep was best when the temperature was between 20 and 28°C (68–82.4°F) \[3\]. It is useful to keep this temperature range in mind, but remember that the season and humidity also play a role in how you experience temperature. In addition, remember that everyone is different, so the optimal temperature for one person may not be the same for another. Women, for example, are more sensitive to temperature changes and tend to prefer higher temperatures compared to men \[4\].

sections.heading: Can Temperature Fluctuations at Night Affect Sleep?
paragraphs: Even brief exposure to temperatures that are too hot or too cold during sleep can result in sleep disruption. Temperatures higher and lower than the optimal range increase the amount of time it takes for people to fall asleep, which is known as sleep onset latency (SOL). In addition, higher room temperatures decrease the total amount of sleep. When people sleeping in warm rooms were asked about their sleep, they reported feeling that they did not sleep very well \[5\].

A thermal environment that is either warmer or cooler than the optimal range can increase wakefulness during the night. Warmer temperatures can disrupt both SWS and REM sleep and cause wakefulness, whereas colder temperatures mainly affect REM sleep. Waking up too many times at night interferes with sleep and all the processes that benefit from it. If a person wakes up during the night when they are supposed to be sleeping, we say that their sleep efficiency is low. Sleep efficiency is highest when temperatures are within the optimal range compared with temperatures above or below that range \[6\].

Why is REM sleep easier to disrupt with fluctuations in temperature? It turns out that during REM, in addition to brain activity and rapid eye movement, people also experience muscle paralysis, called atonia. Because of atonia during REM, your body cannot respond to changes in temperature by shivering or sweating as it would during NREM sleep or wakefulness. Also, the brain area responsible for sensing and adjusting temperature is less sensitive during REM. That means that people are more susceptible to temperature changes that happen during REM, compared to other stages of sleep \[7\].

sections.heading: Temperature Before Sleep
paragraphs: How about the effects of temperature before bedtime? In a clever study, researchers had participants spend 30 min before sleep in three different temperatures: 23°C/73.4°F, 26°C/78.8°F, or 29°C/84.2°F. Then, the participants slept in a room set at 24°C/75.2°F. The researchers recorded the participants’ brain waves using special equipment to confirm when participants were asleep. The following day, the researchers asked the participants questions about their sleep. The researchers used both sources of information to understand how exposure to different temperatures affected people’s sleep.

So, what did they find? Participants who spent the half-hour before sleep in the higher temperature (29°C/84.2°F) not only slept more, but they also fell asleep faster and woke up less during the night. When asked, the participants reported feeling more satisfied with their sleep and experiencing less difficulty waking up in the morning. In contrast, those exposed to the other two conditions took longer to fall asleep, woke up more times during the night, and slept less overall \[8\].

You may be interested to know that other mammals often engage in thermoregulatory behaviors before sleeping too, including shelter-seeking, nest-building, and curling up. For example, cats often curl up on a warm blanket or cushion. Mice build warmer nests as the temperature of their environment drops, and they tend to favor moderately warm sleeping environments of around 27–30°C (80.6–86°F). Similarly, chimpanzees choose shelters based on their warmth, and they have also been shown to increase the insulating material of their nests during colder weather. In humans, examples of thermoregulatory behaviors include taking a warm bath, sitting by a fire, putting on fleecy pajamas and warm socks, and curling up in bed with some warm blankets or a duvet \[9\].

sections.heading: How Does Temperature Actually Affect Sleep?
paragraphs: Temperature and sleep clearly go hand in hand, but why? It turns out that the brain area involved in sleep, the hypothalamus, is the same area that controls body temperature.

Humans maintain their body temperature at around 37°C (98.6°F). Although the specific temperature fluctuates slightly, it is generally higher during the day and starts to decline in the evening. Sleep is more likely to happen when your hypothalamus senses this decline in your body temperature. The drop in body temperature happens when there is heat loss from the skin on your hands and legs. As the temperature drops more and more, the hypothalamus senses this decline and the neurons responsible for sleep are activated to cause sleep \[9\].

By creating a warmer sleep environment before sleep, you help to warm up your body and start the process of heat loss from your hands and feet. That is how you help activate the specific groups of brain cells in the hypothalamus, which help you fall asleep. The temperature in the room and the bedding can interfere with this process by making heat loss more difficult, and thus disrupting your sleep \[10\].

sections.heading: How Can You Sleep Better With Temperature In Mind?
paragraphs: Creating a sleep environment with the right temperature can be just as important for good sleep as having a regular bedtime routine. Temperature fluctuations can have negative consequences, like increasing the time it takes to fall asleep and reducing total sleep time, particularly REM sleep. Engaging in thermoregulatory behaviors before bed may help you set the right temperature. Curling up with a warm blanket and wearing appropriate clothing can help create the right level of warmth to shorten your journey into sleep. Similarly, keeping the bedroom cool with ventilation in the summer can help prevent sleep disruption. As climate change affects more and more people, it is important to be aware of the impact of temperature on sleep.
